summary.text: Set \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\) and choose an arbitrarily large prime \(p\); the only admissible integers up to \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), so \(a(p)=2\). For \(p\ge100\), \(\log p>4\), hence \((\log p)^{1/2}>2\), contradicting the claimed eventual lower bound.

full_proof.text:
Let \[ a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime divisor of }k\text{ divides }n\}. \] We prove that the asserted eventual lower bound is false. First observe that for every prime number \(p\), \[ a(p)=2. \] Indeed, the only prime divisor of \(p\) is \(p\) itself. The integers \(1\) and \(p\) are both counted: \(1\) has no prime divisors, and the sole prime divisor of \(p\) is of course a divisor of \(p\). Conversely, suppose that \(1\le k\le p\) is counted. If \(k=1\), there is nothing more to prove. If \(k>1\), then \(k\) has a prime divisor \(q\). Since every prime divisor of \(k\) must divide \(p\), and \(p\) is prime, we must have \(q=p\). Thus \(p\mid k\). Because \(k\) is positive and \(k\le p\), this forces \(k=p\). Hence precisely \(1\) and \(p\) are counted, proving \(a(p)=2\). Now suppose, for contradiction, that the conjectured assertion holds: \[ \forall \epsilon>0\ \exists N\in\mathbb N\ \forall n\ge N, \qquad (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\le a(n). \] Take \[ \epsilon=\frac12. \] The assertion then gives some \(N\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge N\), \[ (\log n)^{1/2}\le a(n). \] Choose a prime \(p\ge \max\{N,100\}\). Such a prime exists. For completeness, this can be seen directly from Euclid's argument. If \(M=\max\{N,100\}\), take any prime divisor \(p\) of \[ (M+1)!+1. \] No prime at most \(M+1\) can divide this number, since every such prime divides \((M+1)!\), and a common divisor of \((M+1)!\) and \((M+1)!+1\) would divide \(1\). Therefore \(p>M+1\), and in particular \(p\ge M\). We next show that \(\log p>4\). It is enough to note that \[ e^4<81<100\le p. \] Here the elementary estimate \(e<3\) gives \(e^4<3^4=81\). One quick justification of \(e<3\) is the series expansion \[ e=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac1{k!} =2+\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac1{k!}. \] For \(k\ge2\), one has \(k!\ge 2^{k-1}\), and the inequality is strict for at least one term (for example, \(3!=6>4\)). Consequently \[ \sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac1{k!} <\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac1{2^{k-1}}=1, \] so \(e<3\), as claimed. Since the exponential function is strictly increasing, the inequality \[ e^4=\exp(4)

0\), one has \[ a(n)\ge(\log n)^{1-\epsilon} \] for all sufficiently large \(n\). In fact, the obstruction is stronger: along the unbounded sequence of prime arguments, \(a(p)=2\), whereas \((\log p)^{1/2}\) tends to infinity.
